title: Media Type Specifications and Registration Procedures
summary: Defines the procedures for specifying and registering media types, such as those used in HTTP and MIME, with IANA. It sets out the registration trees, the rules for naming types, and how new types are reviewed. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6838 sets rules for naming and registering media types such as image or text formats. It explains what a registration must document, who reviews it, and how the registry can be updated.

subtitle: The rules for defining media types and registering them with IANA.

tldr.problem: Internet protocols need public, unambiguous labels for the kinds of content they carry, along with a process for defining those labels and their formats.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines registration trees, naming and documentation requirements, review procedures, a registration template, and a separate process for structured syntax suffixes.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6838 is Best Current Practice BCP 13, obsoletes RFC 4288, and has been updated by RFC 9694.

today: RFC 6838 is Best Current Practice BCP 13, published in January 2013, and obsoletes RFC 4288. It has been updated by RFC 9694.

sections.title: What a Media Type Identifies
sections.content:
A media type labels content carried by protocols such as HTTP and MIME. It has a top-level type, a subtype, and may have parameters. IANA maintains a central public registry so that names and meanings can be found consistently.

RFC 6838 separates media type registration procedures from the MIME document set because the procedures apply beyond MIME. A registration proposal is reviewed according to the tree where the subtype name belongs.
sections.plainLanguage: A media type gives programs a shared label for a kind of content. The registry records what each label means and points to its format specification.

sections.title: The Four Registration Trees
sections.content:
The standards tree is for types of general interest and has no facet prefix. IETF registrations require IESG approval and an RFC; registrations from recognized standards organizations use a formal specification and expert review. The vendor tree uses vnd. for types associated with publicly available products, and the personal tree uses prs. for experimental or non-commercial types.

The unregistered x. tree is for private local use, cannot be registered, and is strongly discouraged. New top-level trees can be created only through IETF Standards Action.
sections.plainLanguage: Names are grouped by purpose: general standards, vendor products, personal projects, or private local use. Each registered tree has a review route, while private x. names are not registered.

sections.title: Naming and Format Requirements
sections.content:
A registered media type must describe an actual media format, not a transfer encoding, character set, or collection of separate entities. Type and subtype names are case-insensitive and may be at most 127 characters; the RFC recommends keeping each to 64 characters or fewer. A subtype can include a facet and a structured syntax suffix.

Every type must have one canonical data format. Standards-tree types require a permanent, public specification with enough detail for independent implementations to interoperate. Registrations must describe parameters and known security risks; universal implementation is not required. A type using a registered syntax suffix should use the matching suffix and must not claim a syntax it does not use.
sections.plainLanguage: A media type name must refer to one defined format and follow the naming rules. The registration explains the format, parameters, security issues, and any limits on use.

sections.title: Reviewing and Registering a Media Type
sections.content:
The registration process is administrative rather than a formal standards process, and it allows community comments without excessive delay. For IETF standards-tree registrations, normal IETF procedures apply. Other standards-tree registrations and vendor and personal registrations are submitted to IANA, which sends them for expert review.

A provisional standards-tree registration can assign a name early; it requires only the type name and contact information. Once published by IANA, a registration cannot be deleted. Its intended use can be changed to OBSOLETE, and later changes use the process appropriate to its registration tree.
sections.plainLanguage: A proposal is documented, may receive public comments, and is checked through the review path for its tree. Published registrations remain in the registry, though an unused type can be marked obsolete.

sections.title: The Registration Template
sections.content:
The registration template records the type and subtype, required and optional parameters, encoding, security and interoperability considerations, specifications, applications, fragment identifier rules, contact information, intended usage, and change controller. It can also record useful details such as magic numbers, file extensions, and deprecated aliases.

The RFC establishes a separate registry for structured syntax suffixes such as +json. A suffix registration describes its syntax, references, encoding, interoperability, fragment identifier, and security considerations, and is reviewed by an expert.
sections.plainLanguage: The template asks each applicant for the same core information about a media type. A separate template records what a structured syntax suffix means and how it should be used.

sections.title: Security Information in Registrations
sections.content:
Every standards-tree type requires a security analysis. Analysis is encouraged for vendor and personal types, and every registration must describe known risks accurately. A registration must not claim that a type has no security issues; vendor and personal registrations may state that the risks have not been assessed.

The analysis should consider whether content can trigger actions, disclose information, or expand from compressed input to consume resources. A type must say whether it uses active content, and should say whether it uses compression and what precautions are needed.
sections.plainLanguage: A registration must describe known risks honestly. It should explain whether content can run actions, reveal information, or use compression that consumes excessive resources.
